m4-t1.introduction: See the concepts behind a usable Jira or spreadsheet board: a navigable hierarchy, explicit transition rules and safe traceability. The illustrations are not screenshots of a particular Jira version.

sections.title: Use hierarchy to find work, not to manufacture value
sections.explanation: A larger pilot outcome can group small testable items, with implementation tasks beneath them. Each level answers a different navigation question. A grand epic name does not prove strategic value, and a completed subtask does not automatically create a usable journey.

items.label: Larger outcome
items.detail: Placement registration pilot: the grouping and purpose.

items.label: Small testable work
items.detail: Booking, cancellation and capacity visibility with criteria.

items.label: Implementation tasks
items.detail: Concrete steps linked back to the parent item and evidence.

sections.caption: Conceptual work hierarchy. Jira may use different labels, templates or permissions; a spreadsheet can represent the same relationships.
sections.takeaway: Keep only the hierarchy that helps people locate and review the work.

sections.section: 2. Workflow states need entry and exit rules
sections.title: A board state must mean something
sections.explanation: Write entry and exit rules before relying on column counts. In the practice snapshot, two items remain in Review; one is blocked. Neither has become accepted work simply because the board displays it. A blocker is information attached to the work, not a hiding place outside the workflow.

items.label: To do
items.detail: Waiting work remains visible; missing dates need their own check.

cards.label: Resolve access question
cards.detail: IT reviewer · no due date · needs a next action

items.label: In progress
items.detail: Started work needs explicit ownership.

items.label: Review
items.detail: A reviewer checks evidence; a blocked review is not Done.

items.label: Done
items.detail: Completed under the example policy; excluded from active WIP.

sections.caption: Synthetic six-record board from resources/practice-data.md at 2026-09-28. This conceptual board is not a Jira screenshot or a record of live delivery.
sections.takeaway: Review needs evidence and a reviewer; Done needs the agreed completion checks.

sections.title: Link the evidence without exposing the account
sections.explanation: A reviewer should be able to trace an item to its owner, criteria, dependency and evidence. That does not require public access to raw accounts or sensitive attachments. Keep an editable restricted submission and publish only a safe synthetic or redacted view.

items.label: Work record
items.detail: ID, parent, owner role, criteria, due date, blocker and evidence reference.

items.label: Restricted evidence
items.detail: Approved storage and access roles; never passwords or real student data on a public board.

items.label: Safe portfolio view
items.detail: Synthetic records, redacted account details and a clear explanation.

sections.caption: Conceptual traceability and sharing lanes. The offline equivalent earns the same evidence-based assessment opportunity.
sections.takeaway: A paid tool or a screenshot is not a substitute for reviewable records.

checkpoint.question: If Jira is unavailable, what must the offline board preserve?
checkpoint.answer: The same control logic: IDs, hierarchy, owner roles, workflow states and policies, criteria, dependencies, blockers, dates and evidence references.

m4-t2.introduction: Treat each filter as a testable selection rule. The practice fixture gives known result sets so that a reassuring zero can be challenged before publishing a dashboard.

sections.section: 1. Query the decision, not the whole database
sections.title: Test the question against known IDs
sections.explanation: Start with active work, the stated cut-off and a strict overdue rule. Then check the selected IDs manually. Sorting the result makes it easier to use, but cannot repair a wrong selection or a field the viewer has no permission to see.

items.label: Define the decision
items.detail: Which active pilot items have due dates before 2026-09-28?

items.label: Apply the rule
items.detail: Exclude Done; compare present due dates with the cut-off.

items.label: Check the expected set
items.detail: PILOT-2 and PILOT-3 should be returned.

items.label: Publish with context
items.detail: Save purpose, owner, scope and the intended audience’s view.

sections.caption: Synthetic board fixture at 2026-09-28. The lesson’s JQL is conceptual; verify local fields, project key and timezone behaviour.
sections.takeaway: A known result set is a small but valuable query test.

sections.title: Missing dates are not “not overdue” evidence
sections.explanation: Complementary filters answer different questions. PILOT-3 is both overdue and unassigned, so these sets overlap and must not be summed as unique troubled items. PILOT-4 has no date; an overdue-only chart can miss it entirely.

items.label: Active overdue
items.detail: PILOT-2 and PILOT-3; due date before the stated cut-off.

items.label: Unassigned
items.detail: PILOT-3 has a missing owner.

items.label: Undated
items.detail: PILOT-4 has a missing due date.

items.label: Blocked
items.detail: PILOT-2 and PILOT-4 need next actions.

sections.caption: Synthetic six-record fixture at 2026-09-28. Categories overlap; blanks are missing values, not zero dates or proof of health.
sections.takeaway: Use separate hygiene checks for absent owners, dates and acceptance evidence.

sections.title: Every dashboard measure needs a conversation
sections.explanation: A useful summary pairs a measure with the action it can trigger and the role that will follow up. Validate what the intended viewer can actually see. Avoid comparing people by ticket count when items differ in size, risk and value.

items.label: Open blockers → unblock
items.detail: Ask the owner for a next action and a review date.

items.label: Ageing review → finish
items.detail: Ask reviewers to clear evidence gaps before starting more work.

items.label: Missing fields → repair
items.detail: Agree who corrects records and when to recheck the filter.

sections.caption: Conceptual dashboard-to-decision map; raw card counts are not individual productivity measures.
sections.takeaway: A dashboard is decision support, not a replacement for the underlying records.

checkpoint.question: Why should the dashboard not add 2 overdue + 1 unassigned + 1 undated as four unique affected records?
checkpoint.answer: PILOT-3 appears in both overdue and unassigned sets. Preserve IDs and de-duplicate when counting distinct records; the filters answer separate questions.

m4-t3.introduction: Make waiting, blocking and WIP visible, then use consistent boundaries for flow measures. Averages can inform a trial without promising the next item’s completion date.

sections.title: An exceeded WIP limit is a request to collaborate
sections.explanation: A queue is work the system has started but not finished. In this small illustrative board, review contains four cards against a limit of three, including the blocked one. The response is to help resolve review work, not delete a card or rename it to make the count fit.

items.label: In progress
items.detail: Only a small illustrative subset of work is shown.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Explicit policy: check criteria and attach evidence before Done.

items.label: Done
items.detail: Evidence checked against this example’s policy.

sections.caption: Synthetic reduced board created to illustrate a review WIP limit of three. It is separate from the six-record PILOT fixture and the opening scenario’s larger queue.
sections.takeaway: Blocked review work remains inside the active WIP count.

sections.title: Name the clock boundaries before comparing numbers
sections.explanation: Lead time can begin at request arrival while cycle time starts at an agreed work-start point. Open-item age uses the same start but has no finish yet. Throughput counts completed items per period; it is not a duration. Keep the calendar convention and item types comparable.

items.label: Request arrives
items.detail: A possible start for lead time; the item may wait before commitment.

items.label: Work starts
items.detail: Defined start for cycle time and open-item age in this model.

items.label: Work completes
items.detail: Ends cycle time; completed items contribute to throughput per period.

sections.caption: Conceptual measurement boundaries, not a time-scaled chart. Define boundaries explicitly in the actual system.
sections.takeaway: An average for finished items can hide an old item still waiting.

sections.title: Little’s Law describes stable-system averages
sections.explanation: Keep items, weeks and boundaries consistent: average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput. The result is an average relationship, not a deadline for each new card. If demand, item types or observation periods change, investigate before forecasting.

items.label: Average WIP: 12 items
items.detail: Same system boundary and stable observation period.

items.label: Average throughput: 4/week
items.detail: Completed items per week, not active cards.

items.label: Average cycle time: 3 weeks
items.detail: 12 items ÷ (4 items/week) = 3 weeks.

sections.caption: Synthetic stable-system example from the lesson. It does not assert that every item takes three weeks or that one WIP change proves causation.
sections.takeaway: Use ageing and throughput evidence to review a WIP trial.

checkpoint.question: Can you promise a particular new item will finish in three weeks from this calculation?
checkpoint.answer: No. Little’s Law relates stable-system averages. Individual times vary, and changing boundaries, item mix or demand can invalidate a naive forecast.
